He got close to the friend zone but never allowed us to step over the line. If a new enlisted got too comfortable he would show his indignation instantly. But before he could offer a reprimand to the offending enlisted, we would come down hard on him for showing undue familiarity. He would let that be a lesson leaving it to us to “educate”him. Few officers can walk that wire and still be endeared by the men under their command but still command appropriate respect. They often feel they have to denigrate to be respected and obeyed. The only officers I remember are the good ones who are loved and the bad ones who aren’t. The rest, well, I forget because they did nothing to be noticed either way. Question: To all veterans: What branch did you serve in and Why did you choose that branch?
Answer: I joined the Navy Reserves. Then later I joined the regular Navupy when the reserves didn’t honor their agreement to me. My brother and all his friends joined the Reserves so I naturally followed in their footsteps. I was trained in Aviation Electronics and that has served me well my entire life. I served in a P2V squadron and flew as a Julie operator and a radioman. I found flying exciting and adventurous. I remember the Navy recruiter who talked me into leaving the Reserves telling me tgat if I wanted to fly, the Bavy was my best chance. If I chose a good rating (MOS in other branches) it woukd be all but guaranteed. So I chose electronics because it was the highest rated school in the Navy nest to Nuclear. I knew I could use this after I got out. Hers the benefit to how I ended up in the regular Navy. I did 2 weeks bootcamp in the Reserves. I had made E-3 before I went Regular so I got to keep my pay grade, and wouldn’t have to repeat bootcamp which was 13 weeks. So I got off with just 2 weeks of bootcamp which was fine by me. Plus I hasps a one year head start in pay grades so I was up for FirstClass (E-6) a year before my enlistment was up. I woukd have made First class had it not been for my effective date being a month after I was to get out. I was guaranteed the rate advancement immediately if I had re enlisted but I chose not to. My advice is to choose carefully. You can choose your own path if you pursue a specialty you are interested in and will help you in civilian life. Show some ambition and get all you can from it. Give it your all, keep your nose clean and if you follow the rules you will enjoy your time. When you get out, you will have done something you will never forget and the memories will last forever. I’m 77 and I still receive benefits from my service, I get free healthcare, free drugs and every time I go to the VA I’m surrounded by fellow Veterans of all ages and service branches. It’s a good feeling. Each branch has it advantages and for all the completion between them, in the end we are all brothers. Examine the various branches carefully, decide what you want most and pick the one that best serves your goals. Marines, are without a doubt the toughest branch to serve in for sure. It’s a very military oriented branch. Constant drilling, strict protocols and lots of polishing your boots and brass. But they too have good training beyond combat. You can learn a good trade there as well but you will spend a lot of time testing your physical limits. If you’re athletically inclined, then that’s a good path for you. You will learn discipline and comradely that the other branches can on,y admire. That wasn’t me at all. Never been one to challenge myself p, I was more of a work smart not hard kind of guy. The Airforce, well they too can train you in useful fields. You will likely serve as ground support and only a very few actually get to fly crew in spite of what you might think. Your living quarters will be the best in the branches and we always called them “Club Med”. You can advance as fast as you prove ready for it. So that’s a real plus. You can make E-6 in record time if you work hard. Most of your duty stations will be inland but your chances of getting stationed overseas are pretty good. As far as militarily I think they are on par with the Navy. There is a protocol but it’s not as rigidly followed as the Marines. Let’s just say it’s a bit mor like a regular job with a military theme. The Army trains initially a lot like the Marines. But they have a Specialist's rating that will allow rapid advancement in technical fields. So you can get good training there as well. My brother made E-5 in 2 years as a mechanic. Your duty stations will almost always be inland. But again a good chance of oversees assignment. The Navy is the least physically challenging branch. Once you’re done with boot camp it’s off to your specialized training schools and then off to your duty station. Depending on your chosen specialty, you will serve either on a ship or land based station. I was Aviation Antisubmarine warefare rating so I was going to go where that skill was needed. Either a Helicopter squadron or a fixed wing squadron. I was fixed wing patrol plane squadron. But if in an aviation rating and you are assigned to serve on a ship, you are all but guaranteed it will be a big one. If you choose regular Sea Going Navy rating you can be assigned almost anywhere your rating is needed. Unless you are in a Nuclear technical rating. Then obviously you will be assigned a Nuclear vessel either a warship or submarine. I think the Navy is the most versatile branch with so many different choices and duty environments. You will almost certainly be serving near or on the water but not always on it. This is just my personal perspective and certainly not meant to offend. Things have changed since I got out in 1969. So ask someone more recently in any of the above branches. But do your homework before joining is all I’m saying. Whatever your choice, you will end up very proud of yourself for having served your country and one day wear the badge of Veteran. It’s a members only club

Question: As a person over 60, what era do you miss the most?
Answer: The 50’s. I was a child of the 50’s born in 46. It was a magical time for a kid. We still had horse drawn wagons that delivered milk. Farmers used them to seek their strawberries and I woukd wake up on Saturday morning to the sound of clipity clop on the pavement. Milk came to our door in the morning and they delivered it to a box in the wall with a door to the outside. The bottles had cardboard caps that just popped out. The top of the milk was cream. My mom always poured that off first before we could use it. She used it as coffee creamer and for baking. We still had the old ice box with actual ice and ice was delivered daily to a fold out box in the wall. We never had to go outside to retrieve it. The ice box had a drip pan at the bottom and the ice went in the top. I remember how drip pan would get slimy and needed frequent cleanings. When we got outer first refrigerator that was amazing. The milk was actually cold. The freezer was a small box in the top that was always frosted over. But we could keep more food longer now so there was always something to eat or drink. We ate well. My parents weren’t well off but you would never know it by how we ate. My mother was a wise shopper and spread her money as far as she could. Sunday breakfast was always a feast. Mom made fresh baked pan cinnamon rolls, dad made the bacon and eggs and we could have all we wanted. Mom made her own grape jelly, and poured paraffin on the tops of the jars. She was quite resourceful. She was always baking something for desert. In the summer we played outside with the neighbor kids, playing hide and seek, kick the can etc. mom woukd open the door and yell out our names when it was time for dinner. Then we were back outside playing cowboys and Indians. We stayed outside until we couldn’t see anymore. That was our clue to go home. In winter it was sleds on the sidewalk. We were lucky to have lived on a long hill. So we sledded down the sidewalks to the end. If a neighbor had the audacity to shovel his walk we just detoured around it and over their yard. We heard cries of “We Like Ike” when he ran against Stevenson. I was too little to remember Truman. I knew little of what all that meant but I remember the political signs. We didn’t care, what possible difference would all that make to us. I remember walking several miles to the Ford Dealership to see the brand new 59 ford when it was unveiled. They made a big deal of unveiling new models. It was very top secret at the factory and know one knew until they pulled that cover off what it would be. So that was something we all looked forward to each model year as each new one was different. Today you can’t tell one year from another. But we could tell you the model and year of any car on the road. We had lots to choose from, Nash, Studebaker, Hudson, Desoto, Plymouth, Ford, Cadillac, Chrysler, Dodge and on and on. Many are no longer around today. we had our school crushes. Mine was a girl I grew up with. But she never had eyes form me. But I found love elsewhere. The 60’s ushered in a scary era. Bomb shelter companies were everywhere. They sold them like they sell Christmas trees. They rented a vacant lot and displayed them for sale. We used to break into them at night and play survivor. Then there was the Cuban Missile crises which scared everyone. We had duck and cover in school. Even at my young age I thought that was ridiculous. If there was a nuclear bomb we were toast anyway. Why not just watch out the window for one final hurrah? So that was my favorite era. It seemed from a kids perspective to be a great time of innocence. Which just like everything else must one day pass. Life got a lot more complicated after that and while I have some fond memories of the 60’s, it was nothing like the 50’s ever again.

The blower is designed to handle a certain amount of static (resistance to airflow). If one or the other is too small, it simply increases the velocity of the air in that duct. The downside is when you increase velocity you increase air noise. Faster moving air whistles as it either enters or leaves the duct system. Also, your duct system is designed for a certain amount of built in velocity. This is so the air coming out the supplies has sufficient throw. Meaning how far the air coming out will flow in order to comfortably heat the environment. A main residential supply line has a designed velocity of around 600’pm. Ideal duct systems are designed at around .1 SP overall. As the static increases due to filter clogging or other interference, the blower can overcome around .5- to nearly 1” of static in most air handlers and furnaces. The best way to determine the airflow in your system is to measure the airflow. Either by measuring the static in the system or the air through each duct.

Question: Is it necessary to replace the ductwork when upgrading A/C and furnace?
Answer: It depends on what it’s made of. If it’s galvanized, you can keep it. Galvanized ducts have less static (resistance to airflow) so you can get away with a smaller duct than is called for with a flexible duct. There really is no valid reason for replacing this kind of ductwork if it’s size is adequate for the amount of air needed. If the insulation is damaged or missing, simply have it Re-insulated. If it’s made of tin, then you have to replace it. Simply test it with a magnet. If it doesn’t stick it’s tin. Tin is also shiny unlike galvanized which is dull after aging. The reason it must be replaced is rust. A/c cools the duct. Moisture is attracted to cold surfaces. So once the airflow stops, the moisture comes in through the registers and condenses on the walls of the duct. This then typically runs off the sidewalls and settles at the bottom where it accumulates and that’s where the rust occurs. If it’s flex duct, it depends on the size. A/C requires more airflow than heat. So the ducts must be able to accommodate this rise in airflow. If it’s inadequate the velocity of the air goes up and your registers will sound like a jet engine. If it’s old flex, I would replace it. The newer materials are superior to what was used decades ago. And it’s probably very dirty inside. In this way your contractor can size it correctly. You are making a sizable investment so don’t get cheap on something as important as the ductwork. You will be using this system for many years, so get it right the first time.

Answer: There needs to be a vent somewhere if you don’t want the water in all the other traps from bring sucked out. Unlike a sink, toilets flush a lot of water at one time. That air has to come from somewhere and the other drains provide that at the expense of losing the trap water which you need to avoid sewer gasses from escaping. You would hear gurgling from those sources every time you flush. There is a reason why codes require venting at the source of a drain.

It’s more subtle at 30, maybe even unnoticeable. But it’s happening like it or not. Your cells stop reproducing at a growth rate and start losing ground. As Tim goes by our bodies start to change, hair turns gray or falls out. Our waistline suddenly expands for no apparent reason. We start gaining weight even though we aren’t doing anything different. By age 40 it’s now physically apparent things are different. Less stamina, more sedentary lifestyle. Skin is beginning to lose its elasticity and wrinkle become more prominent. By 50, we are solidly heading for old age. Not there yet but beginning the journey. All the things that changed before are becoming more and more apparent. We begin to see the handwriting in the wall and that’s typically when a mid life crisis comes into play. You yearn to have back your prior your, your still young enough to enjoy those things and probably have the money now to afford that now classic car, or motorcycle. You spend more time in these pursuits. By 60, the fun is wearing off the reality is setting in. Your heading for freshman elderly. That reality is hard to accept. The physical changes continue, bodily functions are hampered by various conditions, things start growing on your skin you never had before. More trips to the Dr. the bathroom, more tests etc. some very invasive. But you now know it’s not just coming you have entered the twilight zone of old age. Things begin to accelerate. Those growths increase and pop up everywhere. Your arthritis which started 10 years ago is no longer an irritation, it’s downright an interference. Your back hurts when you bend over too much to lift anything half the weight you used to lift without a thought. Your muscles ache after a workout, out strenuous activity. Rest is looking more attractive as a pastime. 70’s looming like a dreaded disease. And before you even know it happened, your there. The changes are even more prominent. The look of youth a long faded memory as you gaze in the mirror at someone you no longer recognize. Who is that person, how did they get so old? Now you become far more in touch with mortality. The fear of diseases that can bring it all to an end. Your friends are dying sooner that you thought they would. A, I next you wonder? Every medical symptom knows at you silently. Could this be cancer, am I having a stroke? It’s not that you become a hypochondriac but face it, this is when things really start happening. It’s actually foolish to ignore them. I’m coming up on 77 in a few months so I can’t really comment beyond’s that. But I can tell you, the old Bob Newhart joke rings in my ears. Oh to be 65 again. Because it’s mechanical, it requires maximum vibrations to produce enough sound. So they are heavy on the record to transfer as much energy to the megaphone as possible. Hence the advent of the diamond tipped stylus. It reduces wear on the stylus and increases the fidelity of the sound. Gramophones were very hard on records which is why they too were very hard and would shatter like glass when dropped. The held up surprisingly well considering you have a hard metal needle dragging in a softer record groove. Modern turntables require very little vibration to produce sound because it’s amplified by electronics. As such the counter weight can be set do the stylus is very light in the groove thus very easy on wear.

Question: Should a 4-year-old attend his grandmother’s funeral?

So showing them you care and comfort them is what it’s about. As a result I grew up with a pretty pragmatic view of death. I think protecting your children from death is depriving them of a very key part of life. They learn that life will one day end. Then when they are personally affected by a loss they will be able to relate to the process.
